title: Heptapod Codec
thesis: The visitor types any English, even a paragraph, and watches an original semasiographic script write the whole proposition at once as one semagram whose strokes carry roles, tense, aspect, mood, negation, evidentiality and embedding; they flip the grammar, smear the ink until the decoder breaks at a stated noise level, draw a semagram of their own and have it read, and leave knowing why Chiang tied this writing to Fermat's principle.

axes.name: Grammar in stroke morphology
axes.metric: Count of grammatical categories that the sentence sets (not fixed per word) and that the semagram draws as a distinct stroke operator. A category is one grammatical dimension with at least 2 values (negation, semantic role, tense, aspect, mood, number, evidentiality, modality, embedding, quantifier scope, relative clause, ...); agent, patient and recipient are values of one category. Rater types minimal pairs ('we offer a gift' / 'we do not offer a gift' / 'did we offer a gift?' / 'they offer us a gift'), counts the categories whose change alters the drawing, and reads the grammar spec in the code.
ladder: No feature marks: the drawing encodes word identity only, or nothing is drawn.
Per-word semantic features stored with each word's lexicon entry (such as limbs for agency, ring closure, stroke weight, plural dots, strike-through) are drawn as marks on that word's strokes.

Negation is grammar: 'not' or 'never' adds a negation operator to the stroke of the predicate it scopes over, and no separate negation element is drawn; 'we offer' and 'we do not offer' differ by that operator.

Semantic roles: agent, patient and recipient attach to the predicate at three distinct, documented positions or stroke types; 'they offer us a tool' and 'we offer them a tool' draw different semagrams from the same concept strokes.

Tense and aspect as separate operators: tense (past, present, future: 'offered', 'offers', 'will offer') and aspect (simple, progressive, perfect: 'offers', 'is offering', 'has offered') draw as two independent operator sets on the predicate, and all 9 tense-aspect combinations draw 9 distinct semagrams.

Mood and number set by the sentence: declarative, interrogative and imperative ('they offer', 'do they offer?', 'offer!') map to three predicate operators, and 'visitor' and 'visitors' draw the same concept without and with a number operator; categories drawn: negation, role, tense, aspect, mood, number (6).

Evidentiality and modality: at least 3 evidential values (witnessed, inferred, reported, set by 'I saw', 'apparently', 'they say') and modal certainty ('may', 'must') draw as stroke operators (8 categories).
Embedding: a clause that is the argument of a verb ('we know that they offer a gift') draws as a nested sub-semagram inside the matrix semagram, to at least 2 levels of nesting (9 categories).

A grammar spec table, in the code and on the page, lists at least 12 categories (per the metric's definition) with stroke operator and example semagram each; it includes quantifier scope, where the two readings of 'every visitor offers a tool' (one shared tool / a tool each) draw as two distinct semagrams the visitor can switch between, and relative clauses ('the tool that they offer').

Uniqueness tested: a test encodes at least 1000 generated propositions covering every value of every category and every pair of categories, reports 0 collisions (two propositions, one drawing), and the result is shown on the page.

Reference grammar: one reference page documents at least 20 categories, each with its operator, its rule in one sentence and at least 3 example semagrams rendered live by the codec, every example decoding back to its stated proposition; a table maps each relation of Abstract Meaning Representation (Banarescu et al., 'Abstract Meaning Representation for Sembanking', Linguistic Annotation Workshop at ACL 2013) to the category that writes it or the reason none does, and tense, aspect and evidentiality, which AMR does not annotate, are among the 20 (documentation standard: Cowan, The Complete Lojban Language, 1997).

G0.evidence: LEX entries in heptapod.html carry fixed features f={limbs,closed,w,neg,plural,orbit} that glyph() draws as limbs, ring closure, stroke weight, plural dots, orbit ring and strike-through (rung 1); nothing comes from the sentence. Fails rung 2: 'not' maps to its own 'negation' LEX entry and draws a separate struck circle (screenshot), and 'we offer' and 'they offer' draw the identical 'offer (give)' glyph. No roles, tense, aspect, mood, evidentiality or embedding.

axes.name: Semagram composition
axes.metric: How propositions become drawings: connected figures per clause, whether the layout is planned from the whole proposition before any stroke is placed, how local a one-feature change is (% of changed path coordinates inside the affected element), and how many clauses merge into one semagram. Rater enters paraphrase pairs, adds or removes one argument and diffs the core stroke's path data, reads the locality report, reads the seeding code, and enters multi-clause text, counting connected figures in the SVG or canvas.
ladder: Nothing is drawn.
Every content word of the input is represented by at least one drawn mark.

One clause draws one connected semagram: each content word is a stroke group attached to one shared core stroke (the predicate), and no element's strokes come from a stand-alone glyph function (checked in code); a row of complete glyphs joined by connector lines does not count.
Order-free: the layout follows the proposition, not English word order; 3 paraphrase pairs (active and passive, fronted adverbial, dative shift) each draw identical semagrams.

Written all at once: the layout plans the whole proposition before placing any stroke, reserving one attachment site on the core stroke per argument, so adding or removing an argument anywhere in the sentence, its last word included, changes the core stroke's path data (SVG d attribute or the stroke list the renderer draws); no hash or seed of the input text drives geometry (randomness is seeded only from concept and feature ids, checked in code).
Two clauses joined by a connective ('because', 'but', 'so', 'and') merge into one compound semagram, and a participant shared by both clauses is drawn once.
A paragraph of at least 4 sentences composes into one compound semagram; participants that corefer across sentences are drawn once and linked.
Layout is the solution of a stated global objective (for example total stroke length plus crossing count), its value shown on the page; the same input always gives the same layout.

Locality is measured: for at least 20 minimal pairs listed on the page, each changing one grammatical feature (negation, tense, aspect, mood, evidential) or one argument, the page reports the share of changed path coordinates that lie inside the affected element's strokes (plus the core stroke for an argument change), and that share is at least 75% on every pair.
A text of at least 8 clauses composes into one semagram that fits the semagram field at 1440x900 without scrolling, and the page's decoder recovers all 8 clauses from it.

At least 12 clauses compose into one semagram that fits the semagram field at 1440x900; the decoder recovers the identical 12-clause proposition set when it starts reading from each of at least 5 different entry strokes, and removing any one clause changes the path data of the first-drawn stroke (the figure is re-planned, not cut): the whole-discourse semagram of Chiang's 'Story of Your Life' (1998).

G0.evidence: render() appends one .gcell per token into the flex-wrap .glyphs row, so every content word gets a mark (rung 1); the screenshot shows 6 separate circles in a row for 'the visitors offer a tool we do not understand'. Fails rung 2: each glyph() call returns a stand-alone 104 px SVG with no shared core stroke, seeded by rng(entry.g) alone, so no edit to one word changes another word's glyph.

axes.name: Decoder noise tolerance
axes.metric: Exact-decode accuracy (% of propositions fully recovered) as ink noise rises; the breaking point, the noise level (stroke jitter in % of semagram radius, or % of stroke length dropped) where accuracy falls below 50%; and exact-decode accuracy on freehand samples (%). Rater checks in the code that the decoder reads only drawn geometry, uses the noise controls, reads the reported curves, and reruns any repository script.
ladder: No decode of any kind.
A decode readout on the page lists the meaning of each drawn element.

The decoder reads only drawn geometry (SVG path d strings, point coordinates or rendered pixels; no data-* attributes, class names, ids or encoder objects) back to concepts, exact on every deck sentence and on 20 sentences the rater types, at zero noise, with a pass count shown.
The decoder recovers the full proposition (concepts, roles and grammatical features) from geometry, and the page reports any round-trip mismatch instead of hiding it.
The decoder reads pixels: it works from a rasterized canvas image of the semagram, not from vector data.

Noise controls on the page (stroke jitter, stroke dropout, ink blot) degrade the ink live; the decoder re-reads the degraded image, and the page shows exact-decode pass or fail with the noise level in its unit.

An accuracy-versus-noise curve with at least 8 noise levels per noise type and 200 sampled propositions per level is plotted on the page, the breaking point (accuracy below 50%) is stated as a number in noise units for each type, and the stroke-dropout breaking point is at least 10% of stroke length.
The decoder shows a confidence per feature and returns ranked alternatives with probabilities, and a calibration plot of predicted confidence against observed accuracy in at least 5 bins is shown.

The script carries designed redundancy (a checksum stroke, or one feature written in two marks), and the page shows it raises the dropout breaking point by at least 10 percentage points over the same script without it.

Freehand: the decoder reads a semagram the visitor draws with mouse or touch; at least 50 drawn samples are stored in the repository as stroke files, exact-decode accuracy on them is at least 80%, and the figure the page reports recomputes from them.

The dropout breaking point is at least 30% of stroke length, matching the roughly 30% of codewords that QR Code error-correction level H is specified to restore (ISO/IEC 18004); breaking points with and without redundancy, freehand accuracy and a per-feature confusion matrix are reproduced by a node script in the repository, run without a browser, that prints the same numbers the page shows.

G0.evidence: The 'round-trip decode' pane lists each glyph's gloss (rung 1), but render() fills it from tok.entry.g, the encoder's own token list. Fails rung 2: no function reads the SVG geometry and there is no noise, so 'every glyph round-trips to exactly one meaning' holds by construction and is never tested.

axes.name: Lexicon coverage
axes.metric: Concepts in the lexicon (count in code), share of content words in a held-out English sample that draw without the fallback mark (%), and where the entries come from. Rater counts entries, pastes the page's reference sample (or any 100-word news paragraph) and counts fallback marks.
ladder: No lexicon: nothing encodes.
Preset sentences encode against a stored lexicon.
Free typed text encodes against a lexicon that maps several English words (synonyms) to one concept; content words that nothing can encode draw a marked fallback mark instead of vanishing.
At least 300 concepts, each with a gloss and a part of speech.

Unseen words are composed, not dropped: a documented inventory of at most 80 semantic primitives (in the line of Wierzbicka and Goddard's Natural Semantic Metalanguage primes) and a stored definitions table (hand-written, or produced by the model route and saved) decompose at least 50 words outside the concept list; each such word draws from its primitives, its explication in primitives shows on the page, and it decodes back to them; no hash of the spelling selects primitives.
Coverage is measured: a fixed held-out English sample of at least 500 content words ships with the page, at least 80% of them draw from the lexicon or primitives, and the percentage is displayed.
Provenance: concept selection follows named sources (for example the Swadesh 207-item list plus a cited word-frequency list), shown with dates; at least 1000 concepts.
A lexicon browser on the page lists every concept with its semagram, gloss and source.
Export: the lexicon and the script spec download as versioned JSON carrying entry count and date.
Open vocabulary at 95%: coverage on the held-out sample is at least 95%, and for each word the page shows whether it came from the lexicon, the morphology rules, the primitives or the model route.

At least as many concepts as the current BCI Authorized Blissymbol Vocabulary (its entry count and edition date stated on the page with the source), with at least 98% held-out coverage, documented in a lexicon reference: the vocabulary standard of Blissymbolics, the semasiographic system from Charles Bliss's Semantography (1949).

G0.evidence: Free text encodes against LEX in heptapod.html: 36 hand-listed concepts with synonym lists, 144 listed trigger phrases, 143 distinct ('present' is listed under both offer and this-moment; MAP keeps the later one), a 26-word STOP list; unseen content words draw the rose dashed fallback glyph (rung 2). Fails rung 3: 36 concepts, no part of speech, no source, no coverage measurement.

axes.name: English-to-proposition parser
axes.metric: Share of free-English sentences turned into the correct proposition (predicate, roles, grammatical features) on the sealed test part of a gold set, per route: the deterministic engine, and the model route through labs/assets/js/ai/llm.js; the model's contribution is the accuracy it adds over the engine. Rater types unscripted sentences, reads the parse view and route panel, reads the reported accuracies, and checks the gold files' git history.
ladder: No parser: nothing reads typed English.
Typed words map to concepts by dictionary lookup, single or multi-word, with suffix stripping and stop-word elision.
The output is a proposition: one predicate with its arguments in fixed slots for simple subject-verb-object sentences, shown on the page as predicate(arg1, arg2).
Deterministic part-of-speech tagging and lemmatization from rule tables feed the encoder; nouns, verbs and modifiers are told apart and labelled on the page.
A deterministic role parser extracts agent, verb, patient, recipient and negation for transitive, ditransitive and passive sentences, and the parse shows as a graph next to the semagram.

Model route: one call through labs/assets/js/ai/llm.js returns the proposition as JSON validated against a schema; an invalid or missing reply falls back to the engine, and the route panel names which route answered.
The page shows the model parse and the engine parse side by side with differing roles and features marked, and the visitor picks which one to draw.

A gold set of at least 60 annotated sentences ships with the page, split into a dev part and a sealed test part: the engine modules do not import the test file (only the scorer does), git history shows no edit or deletion of an existing test sentence, and at least half the test sentences come from a named public text not written for this lab; role and feature accuracy on the test part are shown as numbers for the engine (recomputed live) and for the model route (from per-sentence outputs stored in the repository with model name and date).

Parses are scored by triple-overlap F1 in the manner of Smatch (Cai and Knight, ACL 2013) per category (embedding, questions, modals, evidential markers), with the model's gain over the engine stated per category, and the test sentences each route gets wrong are listed on the page.
A free paragraph of at least 4 sentences parses into one compound proposition with pronouns resolved across sentences, and coreference accuracy on at least 20 gold paragraphs is shown.

The engine alone scores at least 0.90 F1 on every category of the sealed test part of a gold set of at least 200 sentences; a router in the code calls the model only for categories whose stored model F1 exceeds the engine's; both figures recompute from a script in the repository over stored outputs.

G0.evidence: encode() in heptapod.html maps typed words to LEX concepts by greedy longest-match over MAP (MAXW-word window) with a regex strip of 's and s and STOP elision (rung 1). Fails rung 2: it returns a flat token list; no predicate or argument slot exists, and the decode pane shows a flat gloss list. llm.js is not loaded.

axes.name: Ink and simultaneous writing
axes.metric: What the semagram rendering shows: stroke model (constant line or variable-width brush), how writing unfolds in time (word by word or all strokes at once), the ink medium, and the count of linked views. Rater watches an encode at 1440 px, inspects the stroke geometry and render code in devtools, measures frame rate in the Performance panel, and counts views that respond to each other.
ladder: Nothing is drawn.
A visual mark (image, icon or vector) is drawn for each encoded word.
Procedural vector strokes: each element's strokes (for example rings, arcs, curves) are computed from its feature vector, not taken from stored images, and the active element recolors on hover.
Variable-width brush: each stroke is a filled outline whose width varies along its length by a pressure profile, not a constant stroke-width.
Simultaneous writing: on encode, every stroke of the semagram starts at the same instant and finishes at the same instant; under reduced motion the final form appears at once.
Ink medium: a per-pixel water and pigment field is diffused each frame on GPU or canvas, producing spread and edge darkening on every stroke; an SVG or CSS filter does not count.
A second linked view, the proposition graph: hovering a stroke lights its node and hovering a node lights its strokes.
A third linked view, the decoder overlay, draws the decoded features in place on the ink.
Edits morph: changing the sentence morphs the semagram from the old geometry to the new by stroke correspondence instead of clearing and redrawing.
Stroke dynamics come from a physical brush model: width follows pen velocity and ink depletes along a stroke, with the model's parameters exposed on the page.

Real-time ink dispersion in the manner of MoXi (Chu and Tai, SIGGRAPH 2005): lattice-Boltzmann water flow through a paper-fibre texture with pigment deposition, at least 30 fps at 1440 px on a desktop for any typed input, and the decoder still reads the simulated ink at zero added noise.

G0.evidence: glyph() builds 104 px SVGs procedurally from each entry's feature vector f (circles, arcs, quadratic limbs), and setActive() recolors blue to amber on hover (rung 2). Fails rung 3: stroke-width is set once per path, a constant width. Every glyph appears at once with no writing animation; the WebGL fbm shader is background only.

axes.name: Script identity and page craft
axes.metric: Counted quantities: the semagram field's share of the 1440x900 viewport (%), lab-content elements drawn in amber at rest (count), stroke primitives in the inventory (count), stroke-rule violations in 20 random semagrams (count), deck sentences whose outline is a closed ring (count). Rater measures in devtools at 1440x900, reads the rule test, and compares deck outlines.
ladder: No visual system: default browser styling.
Site palette and type applied to the page.

On-brand tokens throughout (void ground, IBM Plex Mono, blue structure, corner marks); at rest amber appears only on site chrome (corner marks, kicker line), and in the lab's content it marks only the hovered or selected element.
The page gives the script the stage: at 1440x900 the semagram field is the largest element on screen by area, and no input or readout panel is taller than twice its content's height.
A stroke inventory of at least 8 primitives is drawn on the page as a specimen legend, all produced by one pen model with one stroke-contrast rule.
Original form: the base outline of a semagram is not the closed circular ink ring of the film Arrival; no deck sentence draws a closed ring as its outline.
Stated stroke rules (terminal shape, join angles, contrast ratio) hold on 20 random semagrams with 0 violations, checked by a rule test in the code.

One motion language: every animation the page runs (writing, and morphing or noise when present) reads its duration and easing from one token table in the code; grep finds no literal duration or easing value elsewhere.
A specimen sheet of at least 24 semagrams renders on the page and exports as one image.
The script is the lab's face: the hub card thumbnail and the share image are semagrams of the lab's own title generated by the codec.

A design rationale page documents the script like a type specimen (stroke rules, proportions, contrast, reason for each primitive, specimen at 3 sizes), the documentation standard of published constructed scripts such as Tolkien's Tengwar.

G0.evidence: Site tokens applied (--void, IBM Plex Mono, blue strokes, .bp corner marks) (rung 1). Fails rung 2: amber is not kept for the active glyph; the decode readout .lit spans (--amber2 #FFD27A) and the glyph count (.ratio b, --amber) are amber at rest in the screenshot. Glyphs are generic rings with radial limbs, close to the film's circular logograms. Also fails rung 3: .stage declares grid-template-rows 'auto auto 1fr auto' for 5 children, so the input row takes the 1fr track; the screenshot shows a ~450 px tall input panel and the glyphs squeezed into a ~130 px band below it.

axes.name: Writing and reading interaction
axes.metric: Count of distinct ways the visitor acts on the script (type, select, toggle grammar, damage, share, edit the drawing, draw freehand, read, converse), each checked by doing it on the page with mouse and touch.
ladder: Nothing to touch.
Preset sentence buttons draw their sentence.
Free text re-encodes as the visitor types, with no submit step; a deck of preset sentences fills the input, and hovering an element highlights it.
Select: a click or tap pins an element or stroke and shows its meaning until another is pinned or the pin is cleared.
Grammar toggles: controls flip negation, tense, aspect, mood and evidentiality on the current proposition; the semagram changes in place and the English updates to match.
Directed damage: the visitor brushes noise onto a chosen region of the semagram with pointer or touch, in addition to any global sliders, and the decoder re-reads after each brush stroke.
State in the URL: sentence, toggles and noise are encoded in the link and restored on load, so a semagram can be shared.
Inverse editing: the visitor drags a role branch to another participant or deletes a stroke on the drawing, and the English and proposition regenerate from the edited semagram.
Freehand writing: the visitor draws a semagram with mouse or touch and the decoder reads it into English.
Reading practice: the page shows an unseen semagram, the visitor composes its meaning from the grammar legend and is scored, with categories unlocking over at least 5 stages.

Conversation: the visitor writes a freehand semagram for a proposition not in the deck, the decoder reads it, and the page answers with a new semagram (engine or model route, route named) shown without English until the visitor asks for its decode; the exchange runs at least 5 turns, as Louise Banks converses with the heptapods in Chiang's 'Story of Your Life' (1998).

G0.evidence: The input listener re-renders on every keystroke, 5 DECK buttons fill the input, and .gcell highlights on mouseenter/mouseleave (rung 2). Fails rung 3: no click, tap or keyboard selection or pin; no grammar controls, no URL state.

axes.name: Semasiography explained
axes.metric: What a visitor can state after five minutes: which stroke means what, why this is semasiographic writing rather than logographic or phonetic, how Chiang ties it to Fermat's principle, whether each claim is tagged real or illustrative, and the count of false statements about the code or about real writing systems. Rater reads the page, follows any tour, and checks tags, claims and citations.
ladder: No explanation on the page.
A title and a one-line caption.

An intro paragraph describes the mechanism, a footer tags the codec [real] and the shape-to-meaning mapping [illustrative], and no statement on the page is false about the code or about real writing systems (rater checks the intro, the footer and every [real]-tagged claim).
A legend names every stroke feature the page draws, each next to an example mark.

Correct framing: the page explains semasiographic writing (meaning without reference to speech) against logographic and phonetic scripts, says which this script is, and cites Ted Chiang, 'Story of Your Life', Starlight 2 (1998).
A guided tour of at least 5 steps builds one semagram a grammatical category at a time, each step changing the drawing.
Selecting any stroke shows which morpheme it encodes and the reason for its shape, both read from the grammar spec table.

A Fermat panel: light crossing two media with adjustable refractive indices; the refraction point is computed both from Snell's law and by numerically minimizing total travel time, both values are displayed and agree within 0.1%, and a caption states Chiang's parallel: the path is fixed by its endpoints before it starts, as a semagram's first stroke is fixed by its whole proposition.

Every claim on the page carries an inline tag ([real], [illustrative], [speculative]), and a sources list names Chiang (1998), Sampson's Writing Systems (1985) on semasiography, and Bliss's Semantography (1949).
An insight check after the tour: at least 5 questions (read a semagram, predict a stroke change, predict the Fermat path) with each answer explained.

A comparison view writes one proposition in this script beside 3 real systems (Chinese characters as logographic, an alphabet as phonetic, Blissymbols as semasiographic), so the classification is shown, not asserted.

G0.evidence: Title, kicker and .sub caption present (rung 1); the .sub and footer describe limbs/closure/weight and carry [real]/[illustrative] tags. Fails rung 2 on false statements: the footer says function words are elided 'as a logographic script does', but Chinese writes them (de, le, bu each have a character); the kicker says 'a glyph is a whole proposition' while each glyph encodes one concept; the [real]-tagged ratio labels estTokens() over a glyph count from a lossy codec '2.0x denser', which measures no information. The page also calls the script 'logograms'; no legend for orbit, plural dots, strike or inner ring; no Chiang citation, no Fermat panel.

axes.name: Reach and access
axes.metric: Whether the codec works at 390 px, under reduced motion, by keyboard, through a screen reader, and within frame budget (ms per encode-layout-render, frame time in ms). Rater uses devtools device mode at 390 px, emulates prefers-reduced-motion, tabs through the page, inspects accessible names, reads the ?perf readout, and records the Performance panel with and without 6x CPU throttling.
ladder: The page does not load.
Loads and works on a desktop viewport.
A phone breakpoint restacks the layout, and reduced motion (or ?still) freezes the background animation.
Keyboard and touch reach everything hover reaches: each element or stroke is focusable, Enter or tap selects it, and the focus ring is visible.
Every semagram has an accessible name carrying its decoded proposition (role='img' with aria-label), and an aria-live region announces each new decode.
At 390 px there is no horizontal scroll, the semagram is at least 300 px wide and tap targets are at least 44 px; under reduced motion no requestAnimationFrame loop runs.

A ?perf readout shows the median of 20 encode, layout and render runs for a 20-word sentence, under 16 ms on the rater's desktop without CPU throttling, and the render loop stops requesting frames once the drawing has settled and no input has arrived for 2 s, resuming on input.

Performance tiers: when the median frame time over 60 frames exceeds 20 ms (triggerable with devtools 6x CPU throttling), the page steps down to a cheaper render tier (the ink simulation, when present, falls back to plain vector strokes), and the active tier is shown on the page.
Noise benchmarks run in a Web Worker: 200 decodes complete in under 2 s, and the Performance panel shows no main-thread task over 50 ms during the run.
axe-core reports 0 violations, and a screen reader can walk each semagram as a structure (proposition, then roles, then features), not one flat label.

A WCAG 2.2 AA audit recorded in the repository lists every success criterion with its result and method, all pass, and includes a recorded screen-reader session (NVDA or VoiceOver) that decodes 3 semagrams without sight.

G0.evidence: @media (max-width:820px) restacks the stage; prefers-reduced-motion or ?still pins the shader time at 6.0, so the background freezes, though the requestAnimationFrame loop still redraws every frame (rung 2). Fails rung 3: .gcell divs are not focusable and react to mouse hover only; the SVG glyphs have no role or accessible name.

axes.name: Codec architecture
axes.metric: Code shape of the codec: whether parser, grammar, layout, renderer and decoder are separate modules, whether the script spec is data, and whether round-trip, fallback and noise tests run headless. Rater reads the files under labs/, greps for constants, and runs any test with node.
ladder: No codec code exists.
The codec (encode and draw) runs in the page, from an inline script or imported modules.
The lexicon, stop-word list and preset deck are data tables declared apart from the encode and draw functions.
The codec lives in ES modules under labs/assets/js/ (parse, encode, draw), separate from page wiring, and the page imports them.
The grammar spec is data: a table maps each category value to its stroke operator, so a new category is added by a table row without editing the renderer.
A node test encodes and decodes at least 100 sentences headless and exits non-zero on any round-trip mismatch.
The decoder module imports nothing from the encoder or the lexicon lookup except the shared script spec, so it can only read geometry; the module graph shows it.
A node test stubs llm.js to fail, to time out and to return schema-invalid JSON, and asserts that the engine parse is the one encoded in each case.
The script spec is one versioned JSON file that renderer, decoder and documentation all import; grep finds no stroke constant outside it.
The codec ships as a standalone documented package (README, API, spec version) with no dependency on the page, usable from node.
A second, independent renderer (for example a plotter or SVG exporter) built from the published spec alone round-trips through the decoder, the proof that the spec is the system.

G0.evidence: One inline IIFE in heptapod.html (321 lines in the file); LEX and STOP are data tables declared above tokenize/encode/glyph/render and DECK is a data table declared after them (line 272, after render() at 244), but parser, renderer, decode readout and the WebGL background share one closure (rung 2). Fails rung 3: no module, no test.

history.by: ladder audit, revised after adversarial review
